claims.evidence: This is the rationale for focusing on the M-G1 transition.

claims.claim: Widespread protein degradation occurs during the M-G1 phase transition and is thought to contribute to resetting gene expression.
claims.source: The widespread protein degradation that occurs during the M-G1 phase transition is thought to contribute to this reset (Castro et al., 2005; Harper et al., 2002; Peters, 2002; Vodermaier, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The first wave of mRNA decay is initiated during mitosis.
claims.source: Using our method, we identified two temporally distinct waves of mRNA decay: the first wave is initiated during mitosis and the second wave is initiated within the first hours of G1 phase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data including spline analysis and RT-qPCR validation.

claims.claim: The second wave of mRNA decay is initiated within the first hours of G1 phase.
claims.source: Using our method, we identified two temporally distinct waves of mRNA decay: the first wave is initiated during mitosis and the second wave is initiated within the first hours of G1 phase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data including spline analysis and RT-qPCR validation.

claims.claim: CNOT1 is a subunit of the CCR4-NOT mRNA deadenylase complex that shortens the poly(A) tail of mRNAs, generally resulting in their decay.
claims.source: For several of these genes, we show that mRNA decay is stimulated by CNOT1, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT mRNA deadenylase complex that shortens the poly(A) tail of mRNAs, generally resulting in their decay (Garneau et al., 2007; Yamashita et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about CNOT1 function, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the FUCCI system, an orange fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G1) is expressed in G1 and early S phase cells, as well as in G0 phase.
claims.source: In the FUCCI system an orange fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G1) is expressed in G1 and early S phase cells, as well as in G0 phase (quiescence), while a green fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G2) is expressed in late S, G2, and early M phase (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—video 1; Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This describes the FUCCI system properties, supported by citation and figures.

claims.claim: A green fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G2) is expressed in late S, G2, and early M phase.
claims.source: In the FUCCI system an orange fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G1) is expressed in G1 and early S phase cells, as well as in G0 phase (quiescence), while a green fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G2) is expressed in late S, G2, and early M phase (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—video 1; Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This describes the FUCCI system properties, supported by citation and figures.

claims.claim: FUCCI-G1 fluorescence intensity increases monotonically during the first 6–8 hr after G1 entry.
claims.source: We used live-cell microscopy to measure FUCCI-G1 fluorescence intensity in cells as they progressed through G1 phase, which revealed a monotonic increase during the first 6–8 hr after G1 entry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Cell cycle times of individual cells can be accurately determined during the first ~5 hr of G1/G0 phase using FUCCI-G1 fluorescence.
claims.source: Cell cycle times of individual cells can be accurately determined during the first ~5 hr of G1/G0 phase, after which prediction accuracy decreases due to the increased cell-to-cell heterogeneity in FUCCI-G1 fluorescence at later time points in G1 phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of microscopy data shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: 220 genes were downregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells.
claims.source: This analysis identified 220 genes that were downregulated and 42 genes that were upregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells (using a cutoff of >2-fold expression change, see Materials and methods) (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential transcriptome analysis of sequencing data.

claims.claim: 42 genes were upregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells.
claims.source: This analysis identified 220 genes that were downregulated and 42 genes that were upregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells (using a cutoff of >2-fold expression change, see Materials and methods) (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential transcriptome analysis of sequencing data.

claims.claim: Differentially expressed genes identified in the study were strongly enriched for cell cycle functions.
claims.source: Gene Ontology analysis revealed that these differentially expressed genes were strongly enriched for cell cycle functions, as expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the sequencing data.

claims.claim: Approximately 53% of all genes involved in the cell cycle are downregulated in early G1 phase.
claims.source: Of all genes involved in the cell cycle (derived from Cyclebase 3.0; Santos et al., 2015), for which we could determine the expression, ∼53% is downregulated in early G1 phase in our dataset (>2-fold) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data compared to known cell cycle genes.

claims.claim: There was a large overlap between the differentially expressed genes identified by Monocle2 and the FUCCI-based method.
claims.source: There was a large overlap between the differentially expressed genes identified by Monocle2 and our FUCCI-based method (Figure 1F), and we found a good overall correlation between FUCCI-based ordering and Monocle2-based ordering of G1 phase cells (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of results from two different analysis methods.

claims.claim: Monocle2 computed larger time intervals between cells early in G1 phase compared to the FUCCI-based method.
claims.source: In general, Monocle2 computed larger time intervals between cells early in G1 phase compared to our FUCCI-based method (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of pseudo time assignments from Monocle2 with FUCCI-based cell cycle times.

claims.claim: Transcriptome changes are larger in early G1 phase than at the end of G1 phase.
claims.source: As Monocle2 computes the time intervals between cells based on the magnitude of transcriptome changes, a possible explanation for this observation is that transcriptome changes are larger in early G1 phase than at the end of G1 phase, and Monocle2 thus positions cells in early G1 phase too far apart in (pseudo) time.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Monocle2 and FUCCI-based timing.

claims.claim: The first wave of mRNA decline occurred within 20 min of metaphase.
claims.source: The first 'wave' of mRNA decline occurred within 20 min of metaphase (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1), which is around the time of mitotic exit, but before the start of G1 phase (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on spline analysis of the sequencing data.

claims.claim: The second wave of mRNA decline occurred at ~80 min after metaphase.
claims.source: The second wave occurred at ~80 min after metaphase (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1), which is in G1 phase (G1 phase starts between 15 and 30 min after metaphase; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on spline analysis of the sequencing data.

claims.claim: mRNAs in the immediate decrease group declined most rapidly during the M-G1 phase transition and continued to decline during the first 2–3 hr of G1 phase.
claims.source: Plotting the average slope over time for both groups revealed that the mRNAs in the immediate decrease group declined most rapidly during the M-G1 phase transition and continued to decline during the first 2–3 hr of G1 phase (Figure 2B, red lines), whereas the mRNAs in the delayed decrease group mostly declined between 1 and 4 hr after the start of G1 phase (Figure 2B, blue lines).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: mRNAs in the delayed decrease group mostly declined between 1 and 4 hr after the start of G1 phase.
claims.source: Plotting the average slope over time for both groups revealed that the mRNAs in the immediate decrease group declined most rapidly during the M-G1 phase transition and continued to decline during the first 2–3 hr of G1 phase (Figure 2B, red lines), whereas the mRNAs in the delayed decrease group mostly declined between 1 and 4 hr after the start of G1 phase (Figure 2B, blue lines).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Most mRNAs reached a new steady-state level at later times (>8 hr) in G1 phase.
claims.source: For both groups, the slopes of individual mRNAs were mostly centered around zero at later times (>8 hr) in G1 phase, demonstrating that most mRNAs reached a new steady-state level at later time points in G1 phase.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR validation confirmed two distinct waves of mRNA decline.
claims.source: Consistent with the RNA sequencing data, we observed two distinct waves of mRNA decline by RT-qPCR (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments validating the sequencing results.

claims.claim: TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels significantly decrease as early as anaphase.
claims.source: Quantification of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels at various stages of mitosis revealed a significant decrease in mRNA levels as early as anaphase, and a further decrease in telophase for both genes (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This is based on smFISH experiments shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels show a further decrease in telophase.
claims.source: Quantification of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels at various stages of mitosis revealed a significant decrease in mRNA levels as early as anaphase, and a further decrease in telophase for both genes (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This is based on smFISH experiments shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The levels of all five genes belonging to the immediate decrease group decline as cells move beyond metaphase.
claims.source: RT-qPCR analysis revealed that the levels of all five genes belonging to the immediate decrease group decline as cells move beyond metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The levels of all five transcripts belonging to the delayed decrease group do not decline between G2 phase, early and late mitosis.
claims.source: In contrast, the levels of all five transcripts belonging to the delayed decrease group do not decline between G2 phase, early and late mitosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: FBXO5 and UBE2C mRNA levels already show decline as cells move from G2 phase into early mitosis.
claims.source: FBXO5 and UBE2C mRNA levels already show decline as cells move from G2 phase into early mitosis, while the levels of CDK1, TOP2A, and FZR1 mRNAs do not (their levels increase slightly between G2 phase and mitosis, which may reflect a cell synchronization artifact, as discussed before) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claims.claim: Both waves of mRNA decline occur in cells entering G1 phase (rather than G0).
claims.source: We found that mRNA levels declined in two distinct waves (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 1M and Figure 2C), demonstrating that both waves of mRNA decline occur in G1 phase cells.

claims.claim: Both waves of mRNA decline occur sequentially in the same cells.
claims.source: We found that the expression levels of both groups of genes are highly correlated in individual cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1N), demonstrating that both waves of mRNA decline occur in the same cells.

claims.claim: Transcription is decreased for nearly all genes that are downregulated in G1 phase compared to G2/M phase.
claims.source: Accordingly, comparison of transcription rates in G2 phase and G1 phase RPE-1 cells (data derived from Battich et al., 2020) shows that transcription is decreased for nearly all genes that are downregulated in G1 phase compared to G2/M phase (Figure 3A, see Materials and methods), regardless of whether mRNAs belong to the immediate decrease or delayed decrease group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claims.claim: The onset of decay for different genes occurred most strongly at two distinct times during the M-G1 phase transition.

claims.source: This revealed a median half-life of 61.5 min in the decay phase during the M-G1 phase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).

claims.claim: None of the 10 mRNAs tested showed an appreciable decrease in mRNA levels during 2 hr of transcription inhibition in mitosis.
claims.source: None of the 10 mRNAs tested (belonging to both the immediate and delayed decrease groups) showed an appreciable decrease in mRNA levels during the 2 hr time window of Actinomycin D treatment, indicating that these mRNAs are much more stable in mitosis than they are during the M-G1 phase transition (Figure 3D, compare red or blue lines to gray line).

results.result: The authors developed a novel method combining FUCCI-based live-cell imaging with single-cell RNA sequencing to assign precise cell cycle times to individual sequenced cells, enabling high-resolution temporal transcriptome profiling during the M-G1 phase transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C25-C28 describe the methodological development and validation of the FUCCI-based timing system. The method is well-documented with calibration procedures (C27-C28), normalization strategies, and validation against alternative approaches (C72-C73). The polynomial fitting approach and comparison with Monocle2 provide convergent evidence for the method's validity.

results.result: Two temporally distinct waves of mRNA decay occur sequentially during the M-G1 phase transition: the first wave initiates within 20 minutes of metaphase (during mitotic exit), and the second wave initiates at approximately 80 minutes after metaphase (in early G1 phase).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C22-C23, C36-C39 collectively demonstrate two waves of mRNA decay through multiple independent methods: spline analysis of scRNA-seq data (C36-C37), RT-qPCR validation (C41), and mathematical modeling (C50). The convergence of these approaches with consistent timing provides strong support for this central finding.

results.result: Single-molecule FISH and RT-qPCR experiments confirm that immediate decrease genes (TOP2A, CDK1, FBXO5, UBE2C, FZR1) decline during mitotic exit, while delayed decrease genes do not decline until G1 phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 provide orthogonal validation of the two waves using smFISH (C42-C43) and RT-qPCR across mitotic stages (C44-C46). The data show significant decreases in immediate decrease genes during anaphase/telophase while delayed decrease genes remain stable, supporting the temporal distinction between the two waves.

results.result: Both waves of mRNA decay occur sequentially in the same cells entering G1 phase (rather than representing distinct cell populations entering G1 versus G0).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 address a critical alternative explanation. C47 uses p53 knockout cells that exclusively enter G1 to show both waves occur in cycling cells. C48 demonstrates high correlation between immediate and delayed decrease gene expression in individual cells, ruling out the possibility that the two waves represent different cell populations.

results.result: mRNA decay during the M-G1 transition is driven by active degradation mechanisms rather than transcriptional inhibition alone, as evidenced by substantially shorter mRNA half-lives (median 61.5 min) during M-G1 compared to asynchronous cells and high mRNA stability in mitosis, G2, and late G1 phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 establish active decay through multiple lines of evidence: transcription is reduced for nearly all downregulated genes (C49), computed half-lives are much shorter during M-G1 than in asynchronous cells (C51-C52), and transcription inhibition experiments show mRNAs are stable in mitosis, G2, and late G1 but unstable during M-G1 transition (C54-C56). This comprehensive analysis strongly supports active, scheduled degradation.

results.result: CNOT1, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, contributes to mRNA decay during both waves of the M-G1 phase transition, as demonstrated by increased mRNA abundance in CNOT1-depleted cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C60-C62, C66, C68-C69 demonstrate CNOT1's role through siRNA and CRISPRi depletion experiments. While the effects are modest (20-25% increase for TOP2A/CDK1 in telophase, C61; small but reproducible effects for 8/10 genes tested, C68), the authors acknowledge this limitation is likely due to incomplete depletion while maintaining cycling cells (C87). The consistency across multiple genes and both waves supports CNOT1's involvement.

results.result: Transcripts subject to decay during the M-G1 transition have significantly shorter poly(A) tails in mitosis compared to control genes, with immediate decrease genes showing the most pronounced shortening (median 58 vs 79 nucleotides).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65, C85 are based on re-analysis of published poly(A) tail data. The analysis shows statistically significant differences in poly(A) tail length that are specific to mitosis (C65), providing mechanistic insight into how CNOT1-dependent deadenylation may mark transcripts for decay. The re-analysis approach is appropriate and the findings are consistent with the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Differential transcriptome analysis identified 220 downregulated and 42 upregulated genes during the M-G1 transition, with strong enrichment for cell cycle functions. The FUCCI-based method shows good correlation with Monocle2 trajectory inference but provides more accurate temporal resolution in early G1 phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 describe the transcriptome analysis results. The identification of differentially expressed genes is well-supported by the data (C29-C30), with appropriate validation through Gene Ontology analysis (C31) and comparison with known cell cycle genes (C32). The comparison with Monocle2 (C33-C35) demonstrates both convergence and the advantages of the FUCCI-based approach for temporal resolution.

results.result: Scheduled mRNA decay represents an additional mechanism, alongside protein degradation and transcriptional control, that helps reset gene expression following cell division by preventing carry-over of G2/M transcripts into the next cell cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C75-C77, C80 represent the main biological conclusion of the study. This conclusion is well-supported by the collective evidence showing: (1) active decay mechanisms during M-G1 (C57), (2) high mRNA stability outside this window (C76), and (3) the inference that transcriptional inhibition alone would lead to significant transcript carry-over (C77). The conclusion appropriately integrates the experimental findings.

results.result: The two waves of mRNA decay may be regulated by distinct mechanisms involving different RNA-binding proteins that recruit CNOT1 to specific transcript sets, though additional decay mechanisms beyond CNOT1-dependent deadenylation may also contribute.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C81, C86, C88-C90 are explicitly speculative (using language like 'may indicate', 'could suggest', 'it is possible'). While these speculations are reasonable given the data, they represent hypotheses for future work rather than demonstrated findings. The modest effects of CNOT1 depletion (C87) and the observation of two waves both stimulated by CNOT1 (C89) suggest additional complexity that requires further investigation.

results.result: Continued expression of G2/M genes in G1 phase may perturb normal cell cycle progression and potentially contribute to cellular transformation.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is explicitly speculative and based on inference from the data combined with cited literature. While the speculation is reasonable given that many downregulated genes have cell cycle control functions, the manuscript does not provide direct experimental evidence for this functional consequence. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: The manuscript provides appropriate context from prior work on cell cycle regulation, mRNA decay mechanisms, and limitations of existing methods for studying cell cycle dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C6-C18, C21, C24, C58-C59, C70-C71, C74, C78, C82-C84 represent background knowledge and citations to prior work. These claims appropriately contextualize the current study and are supported by the cited literature. The characterization of prior work appears accurate and provides proper motivation for the current study.

results.result: The M-G1 phase transition was selected for study because gene expression needs to be reset after cell division.
results.evaluation: Claim C20 provides the rationale for focusing on the M-G1 transition. This rationale is reasonable and well-supported by the cited literature on protein degradation during this transition (C21) and the known importance of resetting gene expression after division.

results.result: Most mRNAs reached a new steady-state level at later times (>8 hr) in G1 phase.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is based on analysis showing that slopes of individual mRNAs center around zero at later G1 time points. This observation is consistent with the data and supports the interpretation that the decay process is complete by this time, with mRNAs reaching new steady-state levels.
